_what: Which approved cover belongs on which blocked Kindle title, and the evidence that says so.
_why: Seven approved JPGs carry slugs (credit-dispute.jpg). Seven blocked kdp_titles rows carry opaque
Amazon references (A2C99P6JESFOP0) with a NULL label. Nothing joined them, so the only available
join was slug-similarity — a guess that would look perfectly clean in a log and could put the
landlord-reference cover on the credit-dispute book. Uploading the wrong cover onto the wrong
book is a worse outcome than publishing nothing, so the join is recorded here, from evidence,
once, and re-verified at run time rather than re-derived by guessing.
_method: TWO INDEPENDENT FIELDS HAD TO AGREE, AND THEY DO, 7 FOR 7.
1. Amazon's own bookshelf, read through Simone's headless Chrome profile on 2026-09-11. Each
row's anchors carry the title id in the path (/title-setup/kindle/<id>/details), and the same
row carries the book's title text and its contributor. That gives title_ref -> title + author
from Amazon itself rather than from anything this repository believes.
2. The approved cover images, read directly. Every one prints its book title and its author on
the artwork. That gives cover file -> title + author with no inference at all.
The author field is the second, independent check and it is what makes this safe rather than
merely plausible: two of the seven are by Lanae Taylor and five by S. Taylor, and the split on
the covers matches the split on the bookshelf exactly. A slug-similarity pairing would have had
no way to notice if it were wrong; this one would.
3. Byte counts. judgement_assets for jdg_m237hjk7wwc68hyj declares seven labelled assets with
byte counts, and each matches the file on disk exactly. So the artifact she looked at, her
Inbox, R2 and ~/.boss-os/kdp/covers/final/ are all the same bytes. kdp-publish.mjs fetches
from R2 — literally what her Inbox rendered — and refuses on any byte-count mismatch.
_re_verified_at_run_time: kdp-publish.mjs does not trust this file on its own. Before it uploads anything it reads the
live bookshelf and checks that the title_ref below still carries the `title` and `author`
recorded here. A title renamed, retitled or replaced on Amazon's side produces a NAMED STOP for
that one book rather than an upload onto whatever now sits at that reference.

_approved.note: Approved by the owner on 2026-09-09. These bytes are what she said yes to; nothing is re-rendered.
